items.title: Dominic James "Nick" La Rocca Interview, 1958-06-16
items.q: Well, I'll tell you one was Eddie Rowland. He came up there with Tom Brown's reorganized band. And after Tom Brown and them went back... I had given money to several of their members, fair, because they couldn't get a job.

ctx.x: You don't see anything in front of me that I take notes from, only just from what comes to my mind. That's why I don't have it in chronological order. I can only tell you what I can think of at the time. Maybe my talk may be gobbled up a little bit, that I might put this one before the other one, the other one before the other one. But I am telling you the true facts of this music. It was in Chicago where I changed the rhythm. They had a certain dance team. They were doing a castle walk. And up in the north,…
Can you hold it a second?

items.title: Dominic James "Nick" La Rocca Interview, 1958-06-09
items.q: The interviewee discusses Tom Brown extensively as a rival and 'imposter' who made false claims about jazz history, but there is no evidence of personal acquaintance, collaboration, or direct meeting; the relationship is defined by public dispute and historical contention.

ctx.x: This letter he is about to read now. I've come across it by accident. It will show a man how he spoke out of both sides of his mouth. 1949, he said that there was no other band. Now he's promoting Tom Brown, who is recording and who is a member, and got 30 pieces of silver in the form of a loving cup, like Judas Iscariot got when he sold Christ. Would you please read that article from Mr. Sushant?
All right. This is the letter. The heading is... No dating on it. Dr. Edmond Sushant. No all names there.

Dear Stuart, thought you'd like a copy of these snaps. Do wish that I could get some together with you and Tom Brown some night soon. And deeply, as it says here, I am deeply regretful that you got away without playing a note last Saturday night, even though you gave me that, quote, I got a new horn and can't blow it yet, unquote. I was not going to let you get away without showing those guys, well, they call you Red Hot. That's underlined from I was not going down through Red Hot. Speak to Tom some night soon…

items.title: Dominic James "Nick" La Rocca Interview, 1958-06-02
items.q: Then they had Tom Brown's band. It was a ragtime band. These boys went to Chicago before I did... Tom Brown was a faker.

ctx.x: Shimmer Manor had a band. Who? Shimmer Manor.

Yeah. Or Shimmer Manor. Shimmer Manor's band. They were all playing by notes. And they played in the carnival parades. Jack Lane played in the carnival parades. He hired some men who played by music. And he had some fakers in his band. And he also had some men who didn't play at all. Which they were called potato men. When you ask Jack Lane, when you go there, ask him about the potato men. How he made his money on unfortunate men. He had seven men playing. He played a bass drum. I'd be built and blowing my guts…
Now, what about Lytel and Signorelli and their recording of Sister Kate?

items.title: Dominic James "Nick" La Rocca Interview, 1958-05-26
items.q: Well, there was Eddie Rowland came up there. He came up there with Tom Brown on the second try.

ctx.x: Well now, the bands, they played regular popular tunes. I never heard any numbers that was improvised or worked on. If they played a chorus of different tunes, they may have had a little bit flourishes to it with their own. I don't say they didn't do that, but they were playing ragtime. I played ragtime. And the rhythm wasn't changing until I hit Chicago. Now this is going to be a strange thing and this is why they say the miracle couldn't happen. There was a dance team called, wait a minute, the castles. And at…
New Rock, Freddie New Rock. Yes.
